text:
ACTRESS'S CARROT
PERJURED CASE AGAINST

label: text
text: Miss Lilian Gish, recently appeared in an American court nibbling a carrot, which she continued to munch at intervals.

label: text
text: "Carrots," said Miss Gish, to an interviewer, "are good for nerves, and this one helped to soothe mine."

label: text
text:
Miss Gish, who was followed into court by troops of adoring New York typists, was defendant to an action for breach of contract brought against her by Mr. Charles H. Duell, her business man and recent fiancé, for whom she left Mr. D. W. Griffith and appeared under the banner of Inspiration Pictures, founded by Mr. Duell.
They went to Italy and produced “The White Sister” and “Romola,” after which Miss Gish promised to visit London, but the promise was mysteriously cancelled and she returned to New York, where she said that she would like to “put a hemisphere between herself and Mr. Duell.”

label: text
text: Miss Gish explained her counsel, "has a horror of legal documents and an aversion to reading them. She placed absolute confidence in Duell, and even allowed him to handle most of her financial transactions. She named him executor under will, and made him trustee of her securities. Similar documents in favour of Duell were executed by her mother and sister, Dorothy Gish."

label: text
text: Counsel for Mr. Duell said that Miss Gish had reached her thirtieth birthday, and “should therefore be sensible enough to know what she was doing in sign-ing a contract.”

label: text
text: The judge dismissed the action against Miss Gish, and detained Mr. Duell on a charge of perjury.

label: text
text: "With one exception," he said, "it has never been my misfortune to deal with a case of more flagrant and more outrageous breach of trust. There has never been more perjury committed before me than by Mr. Duell."

label: text
text: “If, as is stated, he has been admitted to the Bar, I will take immediate steps to have his name removed.”

label: paragraph_title
text: ARCTIC TRAGEDY.

label: paragraph_title
text: youn

label: text
text: Mrs. S. G. Clay, the wife of Staff-Sergeant Clay, of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, has died after "being attacked by savage dogs at a lonely police post at Chesterfield, an inlet on Hudson's Bay. The dogs lacerated one leg and made amputation necessary.

label: text
text: There was no surgeon within 1,000 miles, and the operation was performed by two of the Mounted Police and a missionary. The operation relieved the pain, but Mrs. Clay died on the following day, showing splendid co-rage to the last. The tragedy occurred in September last, but news of it has only just reached the police headquarters in the spring mail.

label: text
text: Sergeant Clay, who is a veteran of the Arctic, was absent on a long patrol at the time, and attempts to reach him were frustrated by storms. Mrs. Clay was familiar with Arctic life. Such attacks by dogs have not been known by hitherto. — “Central News.”

label: text
text: Berlin, June 3.—Up to midnight twenty aeroplanes out of thirty-four had completed the second and most difficult circuit of the flying competition, through mountainous, and timbered country. Twenty-three aeroplanes completed the second circuit, including a Daimler Baby machine fitted with two motors each nineteen horsepower, piloted by Loerzar, who covered 706 miles in 16 hours 26 minutes. The best time was made by Polte in a Udet machine fitted with a hundred horsepower Bristol Lucifer motor, namely in 10 hours and 10 minutes. The flying of the third circuit of six hundred miles will begin to-morrow.—Reuter.
